title: Ephemeral Credentials & Service Account Scoping — Hosting Tier Playbook
body:
Purpose:
This playbook defines recommended patterns for scoping service accounts, using ephemeral credentials, and mapping resulting audit evidence into our SIEM across the three hosting tiers (Hosted API, Dedicated, Private). The goal is practical least-privilege, testable evidence generation, and predictable SIEM ingest formats so audit automations and quarterly reviews run without heavy engineering work per customer.

Audience:
Security engineers, platform engineers, SREs supporting dedicated/private installs, solutions engineers for enterprise onboarding, and compliance reviewers.

High-level guidance (TL;DR):
- Prefer short-lived credentials (1h–24h) for machine-to-machine access; never long-lived service keys for production hosts.
- Use purpose-scoped service accounts (narrow permission sets) rather than broad tenant-wide roles.
- Bind role activation to an explicit attestable flow (token issuance event) so evidence automation can capture intent+approval.
- Export a normalized SIEM envelope for all hosting tiers with a few required fields (actor, credential_type, scope, request_uri, result, model/route, hosting_tier, customer_tenant_id) and extendable extras.

Scope and constraints:
- This playbook only covers: service accounts, ephemeral credentials issuance, role scoping patterns, policy snippet templates, SIEM mapping, and evidence automation runbooks. It does NOT replace tenant-level onboarding checklists or platform hardening baseline (that lives in infra/hardening).
- For Private (air-gapped) installs some automated evidence exports require customer cooperation; templates and fallback guidance included.

Definitions:
- Short-lived credential: any token/key with TTL <= 24h.
- Scoped SA: service account limited to a single logical capability (e.g., model-serving-kv-cache-reader).
- Activation event: the issuance of a short-lived credential or temporary role elevation recorded with metadata.

Per-tier rules (summary):
1) Hosted API (Redwood-managed control plane + shared inference):
   - Default: all internal platform services use ephemeral tokens issued by Redwood STS with 1h default TTL.
   - Customer-facing service accounts (for customer integration webhooks) use rotated tokens with 24h TTL and revocation hooks.
   - Sensitive operations (account billing exports, tenant data export) require 2-person approval and issuance via an elevated ephemeral role with approval metadata attached.

2) Dedicated (reserved capacity per customer):
   - Platform operators use ephemeral tokens scoped to the dedicated pool resource namespace.
   - Customer on the contract can request a scoped SA for monitoring; generate tokens via a short-lived cert signed by Redwood CA; TTL 12h.
   - There must be a recorded mapping from SA -> commit ID / helm release so service account purpose is auditable.

3) Private (VPC or on-prem):
   - Default: customer controls key distribution; Redwood ships a connector service that can issue ephemeral credentials locally when the admin enables it.
   - If connector is disabled, require offline evidence ingestion (signed attestations) with periodic manual verification.
   - Provide a policy template for offline environments and an example ingestion shim.

Role decomposition and example matrix (guiding principles):
- Decompose by capability (read/write/model-control/telemetry) and by resource scope (global, org, tenant, cluster, pool).
- Keep cross-tenant privileges separated into explicit roles that require just-in-time (JIT) activation.

Example role matrix (expressed as human-friendly rows):
- model-infer-reader: allows calling model endpoints, read-only token usage; scope=tenant; recommended TTL=12h
- model-infer-writer: allows generation requests (create tokens for streaming endpoints); scope=tenant-route; TTL=6h
- pool-admin: manage autoscale and pool lifecycle; scope=dedicated-pool; activation requires approval; TTL=2h
- billing-exporter: read billing metrics and export; scope=org; activation audited with approval metadata; TTL=1h

Policy templates (snippets to copy/paste):
- Minimal tenant-scoped read policy (pseudopolicy for copy):
  "Action: inference:Invoke
   Resource: arn:redwood:inference:tenant:${tenant_id}:route/*
   Effect: Allow
   Condition: {\"RequestContext.Scope\":\"tenant\"}"

- JIT elevated role wrapper example (intent + approver recorded):
  "Role: pool-admin-elevated
   Requires: approver_id, justification_id
   Issue-TTL: 2h
   Evidence: {approval_ticket: JIRA-XXXX, approver: email@example.com}"

Concrete IAM policy JSON (example for Hosted RBAC system):
- Note: our platform accepts these simplified JSON policies; policy translation layer will compile to underlying cloud provider bindings where needed.
  {
    \"version\": \"2025-01-01\",
    \"statements\": [
      {
        \"effect\": \"Allow\",
        \"actions\": [\"inference:Invoke\"],
        \"resources\": [\"/tenants/${tenant_id}/routes/*\"],
        \"conditions\": {\"request.scope\": \"tenant\"}
      }
    ]
  }

Evidence automation and SIEM export mapping:
Required canonical fields for every auth-related event (these fields are required in the SIEM envelope we consume):
- timestamp (ISO8601 UTC)
- event_type (credential_issue | credential_revoke | token_use | role_activation | role_deactivation)
- actor_id (service_account:id or user:id)
- credential_id (opaque id)
- credential_type (short-lived-token|certificate|long-lived-key)
- scope (tenant|pool|org|cluster)
- hosting_tier (hosted|dedicated|private)
- request_uri (API route or internal RPC)
- result (success|failure)
- evidence_link (URL to stored approval artifact, if applicable)
- sha256_of_attestation (if offline signed attestation present)

Optional helpful fields: approver_id, justification_text, calling_service_version, infra_commit_id, region, tenant_tags

SIEM mapping example (CSV-like mapping explained):
- actor_id => siem.user.name
- credential_type => siem.auth.method
- event_type => siem.event.category (auth) + siem.event.action
- scope, hosting_tier => siem.tags[]
- sha256_of_attestation => siem.event.hash

Evidence ingestion pipeline (automation steps):
1) STS issues token; STS emits credential_issue event to internal audit bus with canonical envelope.
2) Audit forwarder normalizes envelope and POSTs to our SIEM ingest endpoint as JSON with the required fields; a copy is written to secure logs bucket for retention.
3) If the issuance required approval, the issuance flow attaches evidence_link pointing to the approval artifact (Jira/Confluence or signed attestation).
4) Periodic jobs reconcile active credentials against issued records and flag orphaned credentials older than expected TTL + grace window.

Runbook: handling a suspicious credential use:
- Detect: SIEM rule fires on token_use event from unexpected IP/region or usage pattern.
- Triage: on-call SRE + sec-eng triage. Look up credential_id, actor_id, issuance record, approver.
- Containment: revoke token_id via revocation API; rotate associated SA if compromise confirmed.
- Postmortem evidence: collect issuance envelope, revocation log, and access patterns; file an incident and attach to evidence storage + link in SIEM.

Private install considerations (non-networked):
- Provide a signed offline attestation format (compact JSON with signature) that the operator can upload to support portal for automated parsing. Example attestation fields: issuer, subject_sa, issuance_ts, ttl_seconds, sha256_binary_of_signed_payload.
- Include an ingestion shim script customers can run that pushes normalized envelopes to our S3 ingestion path when connectivity is available.

Testing checklist (before go-live or outbound change):
- End-to-end test: issue ephemeral token, call example endpoint, verify SIEM receives token_use envelope with all required fields.
- Negative test: attempt to use expired token and verify token_use failure event maps correctly.
- Escalation test: request elevation requiring approval; approve in test JIRA; verify evidence_link present.
- Offline test: create signed attestation file and upload through shim; verify parser accepts sha256 and links to tenant.

Common pitfalls and mitigations:
- Pitfall: tokens issued without approver metadata -> mitigation: reject issuance for roles marked requires_approval in policy catalog.
- Pitfall: SIEM fields missing or inconsistent across tiers -> mitigation: implement a normalization layer in forwarder with strict schema validation and dead-letter queue.
- Pitfall: Private installs using long-lived keys -> mitigation: default Shelby (install guide) warns and sets up CA-based short certs and example rotation cron.

Appendix: example automation snippet (pseudocode)
- Issue flow (simplified):
  request = {requester: service, scope: \"tenant\":123, role: \"model-infer-writer\", justification: \"async prediction pump\"}
  approval = call(approval-service, request)  # returns approver_id, ticket_id or throws
  if approval.ok:
    token = sts.issue(requester, role, ttl=6h, metadata={approver:approval.approver, ticket:approval.ticket})
    audit.emit({event_type: \"credential_issue\", actor_id: requester, credential_id: token.id, evidence_link: approval.ticket_url})

Open questions for program committee:
- Should we mandate sub-tenant scoping for all model invocation tokens by default? (tradeoff: dev friction vs blast radius)
- TTL guardrails: should we reduce default TTLs for streaming endpoints?
- Approval UX for Dedicated customers: integrate with customer SSO/IDP or use Redwood approval console?

Notes to reviewers:
- Please focus review on the required SIEM fields and the revocation semantics for Private installs.
- Tag comments in the doc with area: infra/auth or area: dedicated-ops so we can triage quickly.
